To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) TMPRSS2-ETS fusions are the most frequent genomic rearrangements and are the first genetic alterations to occur in the majority of prostate cancers.

1) TMPRSS2-ETS gene fusions are the earliest detectable genetic events in PCa and occur in 50% of cases; 2) TMPRSS2 rearrangements are initiated at the DNA level and occur in the context of a complex chromatin structure; 3) TMPRSS2 is a target of the androgen-regulated chromatin remodeling protein, ARA70; 4) TMPRSS2 gene rearrangements are influenced by the androgen receptor;
the formation of genomic rearrangments in PCa is influenced by a multitude of factors, including the genetic background of an individual and the environment in which the individual resides.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of gene rearrangements, and the impact of these rearrangements on the etiology of PCa.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie the formation of gene fusions, which will provide a foundation for developing novel strategies for PCa prevention and therapy.

the formation of TMPRSS2-ETS gene fusions is a multifactorial process that involves the interplay of genetic, environmental, and nuclear factors.
genomic rearrangements, and particularly ETS gene fusions, are the most common genetic events observed in prostate cancer.
there are many factors that influence the occurrence of genomic rearrangments in prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic and environmental factors are critical in determining the genomic landscape of PCa, whereas the nuclear architecture is critical in determining the location of recurrent genomic rearrangement.
genomic rearrangements are not only the result of genetic and epigenetic factors, but also are influenced by environmental and nuclear factors.
genomic rearrangement in PCa is influenced by genetic, environmental and nuclear factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are several levels at which the formation of gene fusions can be modulated, and that the modulation can be achieved at the level of the genome, the nucleus, and the cell.
the formation of gene fusions in PCa is not a stochastic event.
genomic rearrangements are highly regulated events, and are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, as well as by the nuclear architecture of the genome.
